shadow:
Look after yourself first. It is good advice, and there is a version of it that goes wrong. The room gets smaller. You start counting what you have and the count never feels like enough, so the giving gets put off until later, until things ease up, until you are finally safe enough to spare some. Later does not come. The walls hold.

This is what selfishness actually feels like from the inside. Not greed, not cruelty. More like a low hum of not-enough that follows you around and quietly closes doors. You are not a bad person. You are a tired person in a tight space, and a tight space teaches you to pull inward.

Most people read this as a flaw of character, something to be ashamed of and hidden. That reading keeps it locked. It is not character. It is what survival does to a body that has not felt held. The hum has a use. It is the body keeping watch when nothing else will, and the moment something does feed you, really feed you, the watch can stand down. The wall was never the structure. It was a guess about how the world works, and the guess can be wrong.
repressive: Some people answer the not-enough by giving everything away. They hand over their time, their energy, their no, and call it kindness. It drains them slowly. Underneath the giving sits a quiet hope that it buys them safety.
reactive: Others give with the bill attached. They offer, they help, they show up, and they watch for the return. When it does not come back the way they pictured, the warmth flips fast into anger, and the people around them never saw it coming.
gift:
Something shifts when a person stops asking how to get enough and starts asking what they are here to feed. The question changes the math. You were never short. You were aimed wrong.

That is altruism, and it is not sacrifice. Sacrifice bleeds you. This does the opposite. Giving from a real sense of purpose works like a spring, the more it runs the more there is, and a day spent that way moves slow and wide instead of vanishing the way an anxious day vanishes.

This kind of giving has eyes. It is not the indiscriminate pouring-out that empties a person. It watches. It learns where the soil is alive and feeds there, and it lets the dead ground alone without guilt. That is the part that takes practice, telling the difference.

And it carries trust. People feel it on you before you say anything, the sense that you are not after something, and they put down a guard they have been holding so long they forgot it was up. Some of them get nourished for the first time just standing near it. The carer turns out to be a kind of healer, which they mostly do not notice about themselves.
siddhi:
Far enough in, the giver is gone. There is no one left keeping account, no separate self deciding who deserves what. There is just the giving, and the life it pours through, and you cannot find where one stops and the other starts.

This is selflessness, and it is plainer than it sounds. Not a glowing saint, not a person performing goodness. Someone so uninterested in themselves that you might walk past them. The love moving through them does not run down, because it is not theirs to spend. It belongs to the whole field of living things, and they have simply stopped damming it.

From here you can look back at the small tight room where it started. The not-enough, the counting, the wall. None of it was failure. It was the body holding a single thread of life safe in the dark, waiting. Selfishness was love that had not yet found out how big it was. Now it knows, and it feeds whatever still has a flicker in it.
